pos: n. (the chief or topmost stone of a building)
etymology: Hebrew eben ha-roshah, the stone of the head — the topmost or crowning stone. The Authorized Version writes headstone at Zechariah 4:7 and head stone of the corner at Psalm 118:22. It has nothing to do with a grave marker, a later English sense.
biblical_def: Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it. The setting is the rebuilding of the temple by a discouraged remnant, and the headstone is the last stone laid — the crowning stone that declares a building finished. The prophecy answers a fear. The obstacles looked like a mountain; God says they will be a plain, and the same hands that laid the foundation will set the final stone: the hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it. What the people are to shout as the stone goes up is given to them in advance, and it is one word twice: Grace, grace unto it. Not well done, not at last, but grace — because the whole work from foundation to headstone was never a matter of human sufficiency. The chapter has already said so in the verse the church has never forgotten: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. The stone imagery carries forward into the New Testament, where the Psalter's rejected stone becomes the head stone of the corner, and Christ is both the sure foundation laid in Zion and the crowning stone of the building God is raising.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under HEAD-STONE: the principal stone in a foundation; the chief or top stone.
webster_full: HEAD-STONE, n. The principal stone in a foundation; the chief or corner stone.
HEAD, n. The upper part; the top; the chief or principal part; that which is highest.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of any thing; that on which any thing stands, and by which it is supported.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; divine favor toward the unworthy.
scriptures: Zechariah 4:7
Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it.
Zechariah 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Zechariah 4:9
The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you.
Psalm 118:22
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
corruption_summary: The English word now names a grave marker, which obscures the text entirely; and the promise is regularly borrowed as a pledge that God will flatten whatever a believer finds difficult.
corruption_paragraphs: Headstone in modern English means a stone at the head of a grave, and readers who carry that sense into Zechariah 4 lose the image completely. The Hebrew names the topmost stone of a building — the last one set, the sign that the work is done. The picture is of completion, not burial, and the shout that accompanies it is a shout of grace. Translations that render it capstone or top stone are making the same point the Authorized Version made in older English, and the dictionary keeps the Authorized wording while insisting on the sense it carried.

The commoner misuse is homiletical. O great mountain is taken as a promise that God will level any obstacle in a Christian's path — the debt, the diagnosis, the opposition at work. But the mountain in the text is what stood against the building of God's house, and the promise is that God finishes what he begins for his own name. Read that way it comforts far more than the borrowed version does, and on better ground: the guarantee is not that a believer's difficulties will flatten but that the work God has undertaken in him will be crowned, and the shout over the last stone will still be grace, grace.
roots_summary: Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; rosh (H7218), head or top; pinnah (H6438), a corner; chen (H2580), grace or favour.

Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, top, chief; what makes the stone a headstone.

Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour; the word shouted twice over the final stone.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — Spirit; not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

“Grace, grace unto it” — the shout appointed for the finishing.
“the head stone of the corner” — the Psalter's rejected stone, exalted.

pos: n. (the vat beneath a winepress, receiving the juice)
etymology: Hebrew yeqeb, a hollowed-out trough or wine-vat. The Authorized Version's pressfat compounds press with the old English fat, a vat or vessel — the same word that survives in vat itself. It is the lower basin into which the trodden juice ran.
biblical_def: When one came to the pressfat for to draw out fifty vessels out of the press, there were but twenty. Haggai is reckoning up the years of scarcity that fell on a people who had panelled their own houses while the house of God lay waste. The detail is agricultural and exact. A man treads his grapes, the juice runs down into the pressfat, and he comes with vessels to draw off what has collected. He expects fifty; there are twenty. The same shortfall is reported for grain in the first half of the verse — twenty measures become ten. This is not a bad season explained by weather. The Lord names the cause in the next verse and names himself as its author: I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD. The chastening was pedagogical, and it failed of its purpose; the scarcity came and the people did not return. Then the word turns on a hinge. While the vine and the fig tree and the pomegranate and the olive have still brought forth nothing — before any evidence of change — God says, from this day will I bless you. The blessing is announced to empty barns, which is the point, and the pressfat is the measure of how empty they were.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under FAT: a large tub or vessel used for various purposes; a vat. PRESS, an instrument for squeezing the juice from grapes.
webster_full: FAT, n. A large tub, cistern or vessel used for various purposes, as for holding wine or other liquor; a vat.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed, crushed or forced into a more compact form.
WINE-PRESS, n. A place where grapes are pressed; a vessel or trough in which grapes are trodden.
VAT, n. A large vessel or cistern for holding liquors in an immature state.
BLASTING, n. A blast; a sudden and pernicious influence, as of wind or heat, destroying vegetation.
scriptures: Haggai 2:16
Since those days were, when one came to an heap of twenty measures, there were but ten: when one came to the pressfat for to draw out fifty vessels out of the press, there were but twenty.
Haggai 2:17
I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD.
Haggai 2:19
Is the seed yet in the barn? yea, as yet the vine, and the fig tree, and the pomegranate, and the olive tree, hath not brought forth: from this day will I bless you.
Zechariah 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Scarcity in Haggai is read as economics or misfortune; the prophet presents it as God's own chastening of a covenant people, and the blessing that follows as free and prior to any harvest.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern reading naturally explains Haggai's shortfalls by drought, poor yields, or the weak economy of a returned remnant, treating the prophet's theology as a devotional overlay on ordinary causes. The text does not allow the division. I smote you is first person, and the instruments are named — blasting, mildew, hail. Scripture is entirely willing to describe secondary causes while insisting that God governs them, and the prophets consistently read national scarcity as covenant discipline. That is a category the modern mind has lost, and losing it makes most of the Minor Prophets unreadable.

The opposite error turns Haggai into a transaction: build the house and the harvest returns, give and God repays with increase. The prosperity teaching quotes exactly such passages and inverts their logic. Verse 19 forecloses it by putting the blessing before the evidence — the seed is not yet in the barn, the vine and fig and pomegranate and olive have brought forth nothing, and God says from this day will I bless you. The blessing is announced to a people with empty vats, on the strength of his word rather than their yield. That is grace, and it is not a return on investment.

“to draw out fifty vessels… there were but twenty” — the measured shortfall.

pos: n. (a costly yellow spice from the crocus flower)
etymology: Hebrew karkom, saffron, from a root meaning to be yellow; the Arabic zafaran gives the English by way of Old French. The spice is the dried stigma of the crocus, three threads to a flower, which is why it has always been among the costliest substances by weight.
biblical_def: Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices. The single mention of saffron in Scripture stands in a catalogue, and the catalogue is a description of the bride — an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard. Every item named is expensive and every one is imported. Spikenard came from the Himalayas, cinnamon and calamus from the east, frankincense and myrrh from Arabia; saffron requires a field of crocuses for an ounce. The Song is not compiling a herbal. It is saying, by an accumulation of costly things, what the beloved is worth to the one who speaks. This is how Scripture ordinarily handles spices: they are the vocabulary of value. The same substances appear in the holy anointing oil and the incense of the sanctuary, where their costliness is precisely the point, and they appear again in the gifts brought to the infant Christ. The dictionary reads the Song as what it presents itself to be — the celebration of covenanted love between a husband and wife — and receives the long typological tradition of the church, which has heard in it Christ and his bride, as a true and secondary reading built on that literal foundation rather than a replacement for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a plant of the genus Crocus, the stigmas of which are used in medicine and as a yellow dye; a deep yellow colour.
webster_full: SAFFRON, n. A plant of the genus Crocus; the flower has a long tube and a large erect border.
SAFFRON, n. The stigmas of the flower, dried, used as a medicine, a condiment, and a yellow dye.
SAFFRON, a. Having the color of saffron flowers; deep yellow.
SPIKENARD, n. A plant of the genus Nardus; an aromatic and highly esteemed ointment prepared from it.
SPICE, n. A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell and pungent to the taste, used in sauces and in cookery.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 4:14
Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
Song of Solomon 4:13
Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,
Song of Solomon 1:17
The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir.
Isaiah 61:10

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: The Song is handled either by allegorising away its plain subject or by reducing it to ancient love poetry with no place in revelation; the dictionary holds the literal sense and the church's typology together.
corruption_paragraphs: The older error, running from Origen through much of the medieval church, was embarrassment at the literal text: the Song was allegorised so thoroughly that its subject — the love of a husband and wife — disappeared, and every spice became a code for a doctrine. The Reformers pruned this back hard, and rightly. Scripture's own doctrine of marriage does not need rescuing from Scripture's own celebration of it. Solomon's catalogue of costly spices says that the bride is precious, and a reading that cannot say so plainly has lost the foundation on which every further sense must be built.

The modern error is the opposite and more corrosive: the Song treated as recovered Near Eastern love poetry, canonical by accident, with no prophetic or typological weight at all. That surrenders what the whole of Scripture builds on the marriage figure — the LORD as husband to Israel, Christ as bridegroom to his church, the marriage supper of the Lamb at the end. Isaiah reaches for a bridegroom and bride to describe salvation itself. The Song's literal subject is honourable and real, and it is also the pattern God chose for his covenant love, which is why Solomon's saffron and spikenard have always sounded to the church like more than a shopping list.

pos: n. (a deep red precious stone; the sardius)
etymology: Greek sardinos, the sardine or sardius stone, said to be named from Sardis in Lydia where it was found. A blood-red variety of chalcedony, the same stone called sardius in the high priest's breastplate and among the foundations of the holy city.
biblical_def: And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald. John is given a vision of the throne of God and is faced with the problem every prophet faces: how to describe the indescribable. He does not attempt a form. He gives colour and light — the clear brilliance of jasper and the deep blood-red of the sardine — and leaves the One who sits unnamed and undescribed beyond them. This is reverent reticence, not poverty of language. The commandment against images stands behind it; John will tell us how the glory appeared without ever giving the eye a shape to fix on. The stones themselves carry covenant memory. The sardius was the first stone in the high priest's breastplate, worn over the heart when he went in before God, and both jasper and sardius appear among the twelve foundations of the New Jerusalem. The red of the sardine has been heard by the church as the colour of sacrifice, and the vision continues with the Lamb as it had been slain standing in the midst of the throne. Around it all is a rainbow — the sign given to Noah, the pledge of covenant mercy, encircling the throne of judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under SARDIUS and SARDINE: a precious stone of a blood-red or flesh colour, a variety of carnelian.
webster_full: SARDINE, SARDIUS, n. A precious stone, a variety of carnelian, of a deep red or blood colour.
SARDONYX, n. A silicious stone or gem, a variety of onyx, of a reddish yellow or nearly orange colour.
JASPER, n. A mineral of the silicious kind, an opaque coloured variety of quartz.
EMERALD, n. A mineral and a precious stone, whose colour is a pure, lively green.
RAINBOW, n. An arc of a circle, consisting of all the colours, formed by the refraction and reflection of rays of light from drops of rain.
scriptures: Revelation 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
Revelation 4:2
And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne.
Revelation 4:11
Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
Revelation 21:19
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald;
corruption_summary: The throne vision is mined for a code of hidden meanings or dismissed as symbolic in a way that empties it of reference; John is describing something he actually saw, with the restraint the second commandment requires.
corruption_paragraphs: Speculative schemes assign each stone a secret referent — a tribe, an age, a personage — and read Revelation 4 as a cipher awaiting the right key. The chapter resists it. John gives colour and brilliance precisely because he is refusing to give a form, and the stones do their work as light rather than as code. The sound instinct is the one the Reformers applied to all apocalyptic imagery: read the vision for the impression it was given to make, check it against the plainer Scriptures, and decline to be more specific than the text.

The opposite handling treats the description as merely symbolic in the modern sense — poetic language for a religious feeling, with nothing seen and nothing there. John says I was in the spirit and a throne was set, and the whole book turns on the reality of what he saw. The reticence about the One who sits is not agnosticism; it is obedience to the commandment that forbids images, and it is why the chapter ends not in speculation but in worship: thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power. A vision that produces adoration rather than a chart has been read as it was given.

Hebrew odem (H124) — sardius; the first stone in the high priest's breastplate.

“a rainbow round about the throne” — covenant mercy encircling judgment.
“one sat on the throne” — the One described only by what shone.

pos: n. (the acacia tree of the desert; source of shittim wood)
etymology: Hebrew shittah, the acacia; its plural shittim gives the familiar shittim wood of the tabernacle. The acacia is the one substantial timber of the Sinai wilderness — hard, close-grained, thorny, and resistant to decay and insects.
biblical_def: I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together. Isaiah is promising that God will make a forest where there is sand, and the shittah stands in the list as the one tree that already belongs there. That is what makes it significant. The acacia is the desert's own timber, thorny and unlovely, and it is the wood God specified for the furniture of his dwelling: they shall make an ark of shittim wood; and, thou shalt make boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood standing up. The ark of the covenant, the table, the altar, and the frame of the tent itself were all built from the only tree the wilderness had. God did not import cedar from Lebanon for the tabernacle. He took what grew where his people were, hard and incorruptible and full of thorns, and overlaid it with gold. The pattern is worth naming plainly, because Scripture uses it everywhere: God takes what the wilderness produces and makes it the place of his presence. Isaiah's promise then adds the purpose, and it is not horticultural — that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under SHITTAH and SHITTIM: a species of tree, and the wood of it, used in the construction of the Jewish tabernacle; supposed to be a species of acacia.
webster_full: SHITTAH, SHITTIM, n. A sort of precious wood, of which the tables, altars and boards of the Jewish tabernacle were made.
ACACIA, n. A genus of plants, chiefly natives of warm climates, many of them thorny.
MYRTLE, n. A plant or shrub of the genus Myrtus, an evergreen with fragrant leaves.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption.
scriptures: Isaiah 41:19
I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
Isaiah 41:20
That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.
Exodus 25:10
And they shall make an ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof.
Exodus 26:15
And thou shalt make boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood standing up.
corruption_summary: Tabernacle materials are treated either as incidental practicalities or as a code in which every detail is decoded into a doctrine; Scripture gives them as chosen and specified by God, with meaning the text itself supplies.
corruption_paragraphs: The first reduction treats shittim wood as a matter of availability — the Israelites used acacia because acacia was what grew in Sinai — and so drains the specification of significance. Availability is real, and the dictionary does not dispute it. But the text does not present the materials as improvisation; it presents them as commanded, in extraordinary detail, according to a pattern shewed in the mount. That God's chosen material was the wilderness's own thorn tree is the sort of thing Scripture does on purpose, and the whole letter to the Hebrews is built on the assumption that the tabernacle's details were meant to teach.

The opposite excess turns every board and pin into an allegory, so that the acacia's incorruptibility becomes a proof text for the impeccability of Christ's human nature and each measurement yields a doctrine. Typology is legitimate and the New Testament practises it; the discipline is to follow where the apostles actually go and to hold the rest with an open hand. The safe ground here is what Isaiah states: God plants trees in a desert, and he does it that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand that his hand has done it. The wood points to the Builder.

pos: n. pl. (the sloping timbers supporting a roof)
etymology: Hebrew rachit, a rafter or panelled ceiling-beam, from a root meaning to hollow or to lay in courses. The English rafter is Old English ræfter, a beam. The word occurs once in Scripture.
biblical_def: The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir. The line is spoken by the beloved in the Song, and its beauty lies in what it takes for granted. Beams and rafters are not ornament; they are the structure that holds a roof up, the least visible and most necessary part of a dwelling. To say that the beams are cedar and the rafters fir is to say that the house is built of good timber all the way through, in the parts nobody sees. Read in its setting the line is about a home, and a home spoken of with contentment: behold, thou art fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: also our bed is green. Cedar and fir are the timbers Solomon imported from Lebanon for the temple, which gives the couple's house a quiet dignity by association — what was good enough for the house of God frames the house where covenant love dwells. The dictionary reads the Song first as what it is, the celebration of married love, and notes the long tradition in which the church has heard Christ speaking of his dwelling with his people. Both senses honour the same doctrine: God builds households, and the structural parts of a marriage, like rafters, do their work unseen and hold everything else up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a piece of timber which extends from the plate of a building to the ridge, and serves to support the covering of the roof.
webster_full: RAFTER, n. A piece of timber which extends from the plate of a building to the ridge, and serves to support the covering of the roof.
BEAM, n. The largest or principal piece in a building, that lies across the walls, and serves to support the principal rafters.
CEDAR, n. The name of different species of trees; the cedar of Lebanon is a large and durable tree, much valued for building.
FIR, n. The name of several species of trees of the genus Pinus, valued for their timber.
ROOF, n. The cover or upper part of a house or other building, consisting of rafters covered with boards, shingles or tiles.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 1:17
The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir.
Song of Solomon 1:16
Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: also our bed is green.
Song of Solomon 4:14
Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
Isaiah 41:19
I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
corruption_summary: Marriage is widely treated as a private arrangement built on feeling; Scripture presents it as a household with structure, framed of sound timber in the parts that are never admired.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Rafters are rafters, and no movement has laid claim to the word. The principle to recover is the one the line quietly assumes: a house has structure, and the structure is what keeps the roof off the occupants' heads. Where marriage is understood chiefly as an emotional bond, its framing members — vows made before God, the ordered headship and submission of Ephesians 5, fidelity, the discipline of forgiveness, the raising of children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord — come to be regarded as optional trim. They are the rafters. They are not what anyone admires on entering the house, and they are what the house stands by.

The related loss is the sense that a home is worth building well in unseen places. Solomon's couple name cedar and fir — the temple timbers — for beams and rafters, spending on the parts that will be plastered over. A Christian household ordered on that instinct will invest most where least is seen: family worship, honest accounts, promises kept when breaking them would cost nothing visible. That is the opposite of the instinct the age trains, which is to furnish the room and neglect the frame.

“also our bed is green” — the contentment the line belongs to.

pos: n. (a room where vestments are kept; a wardrobe)
etymology: Hebrew meltachah, a wardrobe or robe-chamber, from a root meaning to clothe. Latin vestiarium, a place for garments, from vestis, a robe. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it belongs to the temple of Baal.
biblical_def: And he said unto him that was over the vestry, Bring forth vestments for all the worshippers of Baal. And he brought them forth vestments. The only vestry in Scripture is in a pagan temple, and the detail is given in the course of Jehu's destruction of Baal worship in Israel. Jehu has feigned devotion to Baal in order to gather every one of his worshippers into one house, and the robing is part of the trap: the vestments make the congregation identifiable, so that when the guard is sent in no worshipper can slip out unmarked. The narrative notes the care taken — search, and look that there be here with you none of the servants of the LORD, but the worshippers of Baal only. The account is unsettling and it is meant to be. Baal's house had a wardrobe-keeper, an officer whose whole employment was the vestments of false worship, which tells us how established and how ordinary the apostasy had become. Israel had not merely lapsed; it had staffed its idolatry. The chapter ends with the verdict: thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel. The dictionary notes without flattening it that Scripture's account of Jehu is mixed in the Chronicler's own terms — he executed a true judgment on Baal and yet departed not from the sins of Jeroboam — and both halves stand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a room appendant to a church, in which the sacerdotal vestments and sacred utensils are kept; a room for meetings.
webster_full: VESTRY, n. A room appendant to a church, in which the sacerdotal vestments and sacred utensils are kept.
VESTRY, n. A parochial assembly, convened in the vestry or in the church.
VESTMENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress; particularly, a long outer garment worn in sacred offices.
WARDROBE, n. A room or apartment where clothes are kept.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.
scriptures: 2 Kings 10:22
And he said unto him that was over the vestry, Bring forth vestments for all the worshippers of Baal. And he brought them forth vestments.
2 Kings 10:23

And Jehu went, and Jehonadab the son of Rechab, into the house of Baal, and said unto the worshippers of Baal, Search, and look that there be here with you none of the servants of the LORD, but the worshippers of Baal only.
2 Kings 10:28
Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.
Exodus 28:2
And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as crude and marginal; the one vestry in Scripture shows it fully institutional — robed, staffed, and housed — inside the covenant nation.
corruption_paragraphs: The picture most readers carry of Old Testament idolatry is of something furtive and primitive, practised at the edges by the ignorant. 2 Kings 10 shows the opposite. Baal's house in Samaria had vestments enough for a full congregation and an officer whose charge was the wardrobe. Idolatry in Israel was dignified, well attended, and administratively sound. That is how apostasy usually arrives in a people that already knows God — not as an obvious rival but as a parallel establishment with its own decorum, its own staff, and its own robes, existing comfortably alongside the true worship it is displacing.

The nearer application concerns the vestments themselves. The dictionary does not read this text as a general argument against ministerial dress; Exodus commands holy garments for Aaron for glory and for beauty, and the point of 2 Kings 10 is Baal, not fabric. The warning is that the whole apparatus of religion can be assembled around a false object, and that the apparatus proves nothing. Robes, a building, an officer, and a full house are compatible with a worship God will destroy. The regulative principle asks the only question that settles it: who is being worshipped, and has he said how?

pos: n. (the dressed hide of an animal)
etymology: Hebrew owr, skin or hide — the same word used of the coats of skins God made for Adam and Eve. Old English lether. In the Authorized Version the word appears in the description of Elijah's girdle, and the same garment reappears on John the Baptist.
biblical_def: And they answered him, He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins. And he said, It is Elijah the Tishbite. The detail is offered as identification. Ahaziah's messengers describe a man they met on the road, and the king recognises him from his clothing alone — the hair and the leather girdle were enough to name the prophet. Leather here is the plainest possible material: an animal's hide, dressed and worn, at the opposite end of the scale from the fine linen of the court. The prophet's dress was a standing rebuke to the house of Ahab, and everyone involved understood it. The garment reappears centuries later on the last of the prophets: John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins. That is deliberate. John came in the spirit and power of Elias, and he dressed the part, so that the wilderness preacher of repentance was recognisable before he opened his mouth. Behind both stands the first use of skins in Scripture, where the material is given a weight it never loses: unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them. The first leather in the Bible was cut from a creature that died so that guilty people could be covered, and it was God who made the garment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the skin of an animal dressed and prepared for use; hides which have been tanned.
webster_full: LEATHER, n. The skin of an animal dressed and prepared for use.
LEATHER, n. Dressed hides in general; the skin of an animal tanned or tawed.
LEATHERN, a. Made of leather; consisting of leather; as a leathern purse.
GIRDLE, n. A band or belt; something drawn round the waist of a person, and tied or buckled.
HIDE, n. The skin of an animal, either raw or dressed; more generally applied to the undressed skins of the larger domestic animals.
scriptures: 2 Kings 1:8
And they answered him, He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins. And he said, It is Elijah the Tishbite.
Mark 1:6
And John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins; and he did eat locusts and wild honey;
Genesis 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Hebrews 11:37
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
corruption_summary: Prophetic plainness is either romanticised into a style or dismissed as eccentricity; in Scripture the rough garment is a standing testimony against a corrupt court, and the first skins were a covering God provided.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Leather is leather. The principle worth recovering is what Scripture consistently does with plain dress: it makes it a witness. Elijah's girdle identified him to a king who had every reason to dread him, and John's identified him to a nation waiting for a prophet. Neither man adopted the garment as a style; both wore what a man in the wilderness wore, and the contrast with the court did the preaching. Where austerity becomes a costume — simplicity curated to be noticed — the testimony inverts, and the plainness begins to serve the man rather than the message.

The deeper matter is Genesis 3:21, the first leather in Scripture. Adam and Eve had already made themselves aprons of fig leaves, and God replaced their covering with coats of skins. Something died for those garments, and God himself made and applied them. The church has always heard the whole doctrine of substitution beginning here in seed — a covering the guilty could not make, provided at the cost of a life — and the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness in the prophets say the same thing in developed form. Fig leaves are the perennial alternative, and they are always the sinner's own work.

roots_lines: Hebrew owr (H5785) — skin, hide; rendered leather here and skins at Genesis 3:21.

“a girdle of a skin about his loins” — the same garment on John.
“coats of skins, and clothed them” — the first covering, made by God.

pos: n. pl. (the hides of goats, worn as clothing)
etymology: Greek aigeios, of a goat, with derma, a skin. The Authorized Version pairs it with sheepskins in the roll call of the persecuted faithful — the clothing of men driven out of ordinary society.
biblical_def: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented. The chapter has been listing the triumphs of faith — kingdoms subdued, lions' mouths stopped, the dead raised — and then it turns, without changing the subject, to another list entirely. The same faith that shut the lions' mouths left other men wandering in goatskins. That is the argument of Hebrews 11 and it is easy to miss: faith is not defined by its outcome in this life. Both lists are faith. The clothing detail is precise and humiliating in its context. Sheepskins and goatskins are what a man wears when he has been stripped of everything else and driven out to live where animals live; the writer adds destitute, afflicted, tormented in case the garment alone did not make it plain. And then he interrupts himself with the verdict that reverses every human assessment of these people: of whom the world was not worthy. The judgment is God's, and it runs exactly opposite to appearances. The world that expelled them was the thing found wanting. The chapter closes by noting that none of them received the promise in their lifetime, God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under GOAT and SKIN: the skin of a goat, dressed or undressed; used for clothing and for vessels.
webster_full: GOAT, n. An animal of the genus Capra, a well known quadruped, usually clothed with hair.
SKIN, n. The natural covering of animal bodies; the hide of an animal, separated from the body, whether green, dry or tanned.
SHEEPSKIN, n. The skin of a sheep; or leather prepared from it.
DESTITUTE, a. Not having or possessing; wanting; as destitute of virtue, or of property.
TORMENT, v.t. To put to extreme pain or anguish; to inflict excruciating pain and misery.
scriptures: Hebrews 11:37
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Hebrews 11:38
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Hebrews 11:36
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
2 Timothy 3:1
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
corruption_summary: Faith is popularly measured by visible deliverance, so that the second half of Hebrews 11 becomes an embarrassment; the chapter presents both halves as the same faith and reverses the world's verdict on the sufferers.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching cannot accommodate Hebrews 11:37. If faith reliably produces deliverance, health, and provision, then men wandering in goatskins are examples of something other than faith, and the chapter contradicts itself within a single sentence. The writer evidently saw no contradiction. He puts the subduing of kingdoms and the sawing asunder in one catalogue because the faith is identical and only the outcome differs, and he says at the end that none of them received the promise. Faith lays hold of God's word about the future; it does not guarantee the shape of the present.

A gentler evasion treats these verses as belonging to the distant past — the age of the prophets and the martyrs, closed and admired from a safe distance. Scripture does not permit the distance. Paul told Timothy that perilous times would mark the last days, which began at Christ's first coming, and that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. The church in much of the world wears the goatskins now. The comfort the chapter gives is not that the affliction is brief but that the verdict is already in and it is not the world's: of whom the world was not worthy.

“destitute, afflicted, tormented” — in case the garment were not plain enough.
“of whom the world was not worthy” — the verdict reversed.

pos: n. (the thong or lace that fastens a sandal)
etymology: Hebrew serowk, a sandal-thong, from a root meaning to interlace. The Authorized Version writes it as one word at Genesis 14:23 and as shoe's latchet in the Gospels. A latchet is the least valuable part of the cheapest garment a man owns.
biblical_def: That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich. Abram has just won a battle and rescued the captives of Sodom, and the king of Sodom offers him the spoil. His refusal is absolute and he fixes its lower limit with two deliberately trivial objects: a thread and a sandal-lace. Not the least thing. And he gives his reason, which is the whole point of the episode — lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich. Abram had received a promise that God would bless him and make his name great, and he would not allow a pagan king to be able to claim credit for its fulfilment. The refusal is grounded in an oath he states in the previous verse: I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth. Because God possesses everything, Abram can afford to take nothing. The same humble object appears in the Gospels in the mouth of John the Baptist, measuring himself against Christ: whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose. Unfastening a sandal was the work of the lowest slave in a household, and John says he is unfit even for that. In both places the latchet marks a boundary — the smallest thing a man will not take, and the smallest service a man dare not claim.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under LATCHET: the string that fastens a shoe; a thong or lace.
webster_full: LATCHET, n. The string that fastens a shoe.
SHOE, n. A covering for the foot, usually of leather, composed of a thick species for the sole and a thinner kind for the upper part.
THONG, n. A strap of leather, used for fastening any thing.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; particularly in war, plunder; pillage.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
scriptures: Genesis 14:23
That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich:
Genesis 14:22
And Abram said to the king of Sodom, I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth,
John 1:27
He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose.
Mark 1:7
And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.
corruption_summary: Abram's refusal is read as scruple or as an ancient custom; it is a deliberate guarding of God's glory, and the modern instinct runs the other way — toward whatever provision can be had, from whatever source.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode is often treated as personal fastidiousness, admirable but idiosyncratic. Abram's stated reason is doctrinal. He had been promised that God would bless him, and he refused any arrangement that would let another party claim the credit. That is a jealousy for God's glory expressed in a business decision, and it is rare in any age. The modern instinct in ministry and in life is to accept provision wherever it appears and to sort out the associations afterward, on the reasoning that the money is neutral. Abram judged that a thread from the king of Sodom was not neutral, because of the sentence the king would be able to speak afterward.

The second use of the latchet cuts at pride rather than provision. John the Baptist — of whom the Lord said there was none greater born of women — measures himself against Christ and says he is unworthy to perform the office of the meanest slave in the house. He says it at the height of his own popularity, with crowds coming out to him. Where ministry is built on platform and reputation, that sentence is unsayable. It is, however, the only accurate measurement, and the men Scripture honours are consistently the ones who made it: he must increase, but I must decrease.

“lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich” — the reason given.
“whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose” — the lowest service, disclaimed.
